_about: EPA Table 1 (Water Damage — Cleanup and Mold Prevention) applied per page, with a per-CITY second half built from retrieved figures. Every row is verbatim from EPA with a live link. No source, no row.
_anti_fingerprint: The EPA quotes are identical fleet-wide — that is what a quote is. Everything else varies: the per-city sentence is generated from the city's own retrieved figures via `when` conditions, and the METRIC differs by page (freezing nights on the burst-pipe page, flood history on the basement page, heavy-rain days on the roof page, housing age on the appliance pages, rainfall elsewhere). So two pages on one site differ from each other AND the same page differs between sites. This is the gap mold-materials has: its location notes are hand-written per location and therefore identical across all 100 sites.
_scope_rule: Table 1 is CLEAN WATER ONLY, by EPA's own caveat. sewage-cleanup therefore gets no drying rows at all — it gets the caveat as its content, which is more use there than a drying table would be. roof-tarping and emergency-board-up are prevention services, so they get the 24-48 hour window without a material table.
_seo: Each page has its own question-shaped h2 built on a real query form — 'Can wet drywall be saved in {city}, {SS}?', 'Can a water-damaged hardwood floor be dried…' — so 24 pages do not compete with one another. Table carries a <caption> and scope attributes; quotes use <q cite> and <cite> with the full document title.

wallboard.label: Wallboard (drywall)
wallboard.verbatim: May be dried in place if there is no obvious swelling and the seams are intact. If not, remove, discard, and replace. Ventilate the wall cavity, if possible.
wallboard.context: That is a test anyone can run before a quote is written: look for swelling, and look at whether the seams have opened.

wood.label: Wood surfaces
wood.verbatim: Remove moisture immediately and use dehumidifiers, gentle heat, and fans for drying. (Use caution when applying heat to hardwood floors.) Treated or finished wood surfaces may be cleaned with mild detergent and clean water and allowed to dry. Wet paneling should be pried away from wall for drying.
wood.context: Note EPA's own parenthesis about heat and hardwood — aggressive drying is how a floor that could have been saved ends up cupped.

carpet.label: Carpet and backing
carpet.verbatim: Remove water with water extraction vacuum. Reduce ambient humidity levels with dehumidifier. Accelerate drying process with fans.

upholstered.label: Upholstered furniture
upholstered.verbatim: Remove water with water extraction vacuum. Accelerate drying process with dehumidifiers, fans, and/or heaters. May be difficult to completely dry within 48 hours. If the piece is valuable, you may wish to consult a restoration/water damage professional who specializes in furniture.
upholstered.context: EPA is explicit that 48 hours may not be enough for upholstery, which is why furniture is usually the first thing to lose and the last thing people think of.

concrete.label: Concrete or cinder block
concrete.verbatim: Remove water with water extraction vacuum. Accelerate drying process with dehumidifiers, fans, and/or heaters.

ceiling_tile.label: Ceiling tiles
ceiling_tile.context: The one material on this list with no decision to make.

universal.verbatim: Mold can grow on wood, drywall, carpet and furniture if they remain wet for more than 24 hours.

These guidelines are for damage caused by clean water. If you know or suspect that the water source is contaminated with sewage, or chemical or biological pollutants, then Personal Protective Equipment and containment are required by OSHA.

intros: The first decision after water is not how to dry it but what can be dried at all. EPA publishes an answer material by material, and this is that guidance applied to {label}.
Some of what water touches can be dried in place and some of it has to leave the building. EPA sets that out material by material, reproduced below for {label}.
